proofs.proof_tex:
Put \(p=\mu_1\), \(q=\mu_0\), and \(c=1-\alpha\), so \(\tau=1+c\).  We first prove the elementary sumset inequality used below.  If \(A=\{a_1<\cdots<a_r\}\) and \(-B=\{b_1<\cdots<b_s\}\) are nonempty subsets of the integers, then
\[
a_1+b_1<\cdots<a_r+b_1<a_r+b_2<\cdots<a_r+b_s
\]
are \(r+s-1\) distinct elements of \(A-B\).  Hence
\[
|A-B|\geq |A|+|B|-1. \tag{1}
\]
This ordering argument also covers singleton sets and uses no positivity condition on \(p\) or \(q\).

We next establish deterministic bounds.  If \(k^*=1\), a shortest valid set is a singleton and therefore an interval, so \(I^*=1\).  If \(k^*=2\), \(\mathrm{thm{:}all\mbox{-}minimizers}\) supplies \((A,B)\in\mathcal F_\tau\) such that \(|A-B|=2\).  By (1), \(|A|+|B|\leq3\).  Both sides cannot be singletons because their difference set would then have one element.  Thus their cardinalities are \((1,2)\) or \((2,1)\).  It follows directly from \(A,B\subseteq X=\{0,\ldots,L-1\}\) that
\[
\operatorname{span}(A-B)\leq L-1.
\]
The consecutive hull of \(A-B\) consequently contains at most \(L\) effects.  It contains the threshold-feasible difference set \(A-B\), so it is valid by \(\mathrm{thm{:}all\mbox{-}minimizers}\).  Therefore
\[
k^*=2\quad\Longrightarrow\quad I^*\leq L. \tag{2}
\]
If \(k^*\geq3\), the product table \(\gamma_{ij}=p_iq_j\) belongs to \(\Gamma(p,q)\), so the coupling polytope is nonempty.  Every member of that polytope puts total mass one on \(E\), and the definition of worst coverage gives \(h_\mu(E)=1\geq c\).  Thus
\[
k^*\geq3\quad\Longrightarrow\quad I^*\leq |E|=2L-1. \tag{3}
\]
Equations (2)--(3), together with the singleton case, imply
\[
\frac{I^*}{k^*}\leq
\begin{cases}
1,&k^*=1,\\
L/2,&k^*=2,\\
(2L-1)/3,&k^*\geq3,
\end{cases}
\qquad
I^*-k^*\leq
\begin{cases}
0,&k^*=1,\\
L-2,&k^*=2,\\
2L-4,&k^*\geq3.
\end{cases} \tag{4}
\]
Because the support assumption gives \(L\geq3\), one has \(L/2\leq(2L-1)/3\) and \(L-2\leq2L-4\).  This proves the stated high-coverage multiplicative bound and the additive bound for every allowed \(\alpha\).

Suppose now that \(1/2\leq\alpha<1\), equivalently \(0<c\leq1/2\).  Partition \(X\) into two nonempty consecutive blocks \(B_1,B_2\), each of cardinality at most \(\lceil L/2\rceil\).  Since \(q(B_1)+q(B_2)=1\), one block, denoted by \(B\), satisfies
\[
q(B)\geq\frac12\geq c.
\]
Taking \(A=X\) gives
\[
p(A)+q(B)=1+q(B)\geq1+c=\tau,
\]
so \((X,B)\in\mathcal F_\tau\).  If \(B=\{r,r+1,\ldots,r+b-1\}\), direct subtraction of the two integer intervals yields
\[
X-B=\{-(r+b-1),-(r+b-2),\ldots,L-1-r\},
\qquad |X-B|=L+b-1.
\]
This is a valid interval by \(\mathrm{thm{:}all\mbox{-}minimizers}\), and hence
\[
I^*\leq L+\lceil L/2\rceil-1. \tag{5}
\]
When \(k^*\geq3\), the parity calculation
\[
2\lceil L/2\rceil-2=
\begin{cases}
L-2,&L\text{ is even},\\
L-1,&L\text{ is odd}
\end{cases}
<L
\]
and (5) give
\[
\frac{I^*}{k^*}\leq\frac{L+\lceil L/2\rceil-1}{3}<\frac L2. \tag{6}
\]
For \(k^*=1\), the ratio is \(1<L/2\), while for \(k^*=2\), (2) gives the weak bound \(I^*/k^*\leq L/2\).  This proves the low-coverage branch.

We next prove sharpness for \(0<\alpha<1/2\).  Choose
\[
0<\varepsilon<\min\{\alpha/2,1-2\alpha\},
\qquad M=\frac{1-\varepsilon}{2},
\qquad e=\frac{\varepsilon}{L-2},
\]
and set \(p=q\) with mass \(M\) at each endpoint and mass \(e\) at every interior category.  These marginals are strictly positive and normalized.  For \(A=B=\{0,L-1\}\),
\[
A-B=\{-L+1,0,L-1\},
\qquad p(A)+q(B)=2-2\varepsilon>2-\alpha=\tau.
\]
Thus this three-effect set is valid by \(\mathrm{thm{:}all\mbox{-}minimizers}\).

Let \(S\subseteq E\) have at most two elements.  It omits at least one of \(-L+1,0,L-1\).  If \(0\notin S\), the diagonal table \(\gamma_{ij}=p_i\mathbf 1\{i=j\}\) is a coupling of \(p=q\) and gives zero mass to \(S\).  If \(-L+1\notin S\), put mass \(M\) at the cell \((0,L-1)\).  More explicitly, let
\[
r_i=p_i-M\mathbf 1\{i=0\},
\qquad s_j=q_j-M\mathbf 1\{j=L-1\},
\]
and complete the table by \(r_is_j/(1-M)\).  Both residual vectors are nonnegative and have total \(1-M>0\), so this is a coupling in \(\Gamma(p,q)\); its selected corner has effect \(-L+1\notin S\).  Consequently its coverage of \(S\) is at most \(1-M\).  The analogous construction with corner \((L-1,0)\) applies if \(L-1\notin S\).  In all cases,
\[
h_\mu(S)\leq1-M=\frac{1+\varepsilon}{2}<1-\alpha=c, \tag{7}
\]
where the strict inequality is exactly \(\varepsilon<1-2\alpha\).  Hence no set of cardinality at most two is valid and \(k^*=3\).

Every proper consecutive subset of \(E\) omits at least one of the extreme effects \(-L+1\) and \(L-1\).  The corresponding corner coupling just constructed again gives coverage at most \((1+\varepsilon)/2<c\).  Since \(E\) itself is valid, \(I^*=2L-1\).  Therefore
\[
\frac{I^*}{k^*}=\frac{2L-1}{3},
\qquad I^*-k^*=2L-4. \tag{8}
\]

At the elbow \(\alpha=1/2\), let \(p=q\) put mass \(1/2\) at each endpoint and zero elsewhere.  The rectangle \(A=\{0\}\), \(B=\{0,L-1\}\) has mass sum \(3/2=\tau\) and difference set \(\{-L+1,0\}\), so \(k^*\leq2\).  By (1), a rectangle with a singleton difference set has singleton sides, whose mass sum is at most one; this is strictly below \(\tau=3/2\).  The all-minimizers theorem therefore gives \(k^*=2\).  For every \(1\leq w<L\), a consecutive outcome block contains at most one endpoint, and hence
\[
Q_0(w)=Q_1(w)=\frac12.
\]
The constraint \(a+b\leq L\) in \(B_{L-1}\) forces \(a,b<L\), so \(B_{L-1}=1<\tau\).  By \(\mathrm{thm{:}general\mbox{-}frontier}\), no valid effect interval has at most \(L-1\) points.  The consecutive hull \(\{-L+1,\ldots,0\}\) of the valid two-point set has \(L\) points and remains valid, proving \(I^*=L\).

Finally, let \(1/2<\alpha<1\) and choose \(0<\varepsilon<(2\alpha-1)/3\).  Put \(M=(1-\varepsilon)/2\), \(e=\varepsilon/(L-2)\), and again give both marginals endpoint mass \(M\) and common interior mass \(e\).  The restriction implies \(\varepsilon<1/3\), so \(M>e\).  For \(A=\{0\}\) and \(B=\{0,L-1\}\),
\[
p(A)+q(B)=3M=\frac{3(1-\varepsilon)}2>2-\alpha=\tau,
\]
and the difference set has two elements.  Thus \(k^*\leq2\).  A singleton difference again forces singleton sides by (1), while the sum of any two atom masses is at most \(2M=1-\varepsilon<1<\tau\); hence \(k^*=2\).  For \(1\leq w<L\), a consecutive block contains at most one endpoint and the endpoint block is optimal because \(M>e\).  Therefore
\[
Q_0(w)=Q_1(w)=M+(w-1)e.
\]
For \(a+b\leq L\),
\[
Q_1(a)+Q_0(b)\leq2M+(L-2)e=1,
\]
with equality when \(a+b=L\).  Hence \(B_{L-1}=1<\tau\).  The general-frontier theorem excludes every valid effect interval shorter than \(L\), whereas the hull of the valid two-point set supplies a valid interval of length \(L\).  Thus \(I^*=L\) and \(I^*/k^*=L/2\).  The two sharpness constructions use only the stated fixed-marginal class and unrestricted coupling, so the asserted comparison has exactly the claimed scope.

Write \(c=1-\alpha\) and \(\tau=1+c\).  We use the three deterministic implications established in \(\mathrm{thm{:}sharp\mbox{-}interval\mbox{-}price}\):
\[
k^*=1\Longrightarrow I^*=1,
\qquad k^*=2\Longrightarrow I^*\leq L,
\qquad k^*\geq3\Longrightarrow I^*\leq2L-1. \tag{1}
\]

First suppose \(0<\alpha<1/2\).  If \(k^*=1\), then \(I^*/k^*=1\) and \(I^*-k^*=0\).  If \(k^*=2\), (1) and \(L\geq3\) give
\[
\frac{I^*}{k^*}\leq\frac L2<\frac{2L-1}{3},
\qquad I^*-k^*\leq L-2<2L-4. \tag{2}
\]
If \(k^*\geq3\), then
\[
\frac{I^*}{k^*}\leq\frac{2L-1}{k^*}\leq\frac{2L-1}{3},
\qquad I^*-k^*\leq2L-1-k^*\leq2L-4. \tag{3}
\]
Equality in either chain in (3) holds if and only if \(k^*=3\) and \(I^*=2L-1\).  Together with (2), this proves equivalence of the first three high-coverage conditions in the statement.

By \(\mathrm{thm{:}general\mbox{-}frontier}\), existence of an arbitrary valid set with at most \(k\) elements is equivalent to \(R_k\geq\tau\).  Therefore
\[
k^*=3\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad R_2<\tau\leq R_3. \tag{4}
\]
The full interval \(E\) is valid, and the interval part of the same theorem consequently gives
\[
I^*=2L-1\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad B_{2L-2}<\tau. \tag{5}
\]
It remains to express (5) in marginal coordinates.  Each \(Q_d(w)\) is nondecreasing in \(w\): an interval of width \(w<L\) can be enlarged by one adjacent point inside \(X\), and all marginal masses are nonnegative.  Under \(1\leq a,b\leq L\) and \(a+b\leq2L-1\), any profile sum is therefore bounded by one of the sums at \((a,b)=(L,L-1)\) or \((L-1,L)\).  Moreover,
\[
Q_d(L)=1,
\qquad
Q_d(L-1)=\max\{1-\mu_{d,0},1-\mu_{d,L-1}\}
=1-\min\{\mu_{d,0},\mu_{d,L-1}\}.
\]
Thus the definition of \(B_k\) yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
B_{2L-2}
&=\max\{1+Q_0(L-1),Q_1(L-1)+1\}\\
&=2-\min\{\mu_{1,0},\mu_{1,L-1},\mu_{0,0},\mu_{0,L-1}\}. \tag{6}
\end{aligned}
\]
Since \(\tau=2-\alpha\), (4)--(6) prove equivalence of all five high-coverage conditions, including boundary marginal laws and threshold equalities.

Now suppose \(1/2\leq\alpha<1\).  The low-coverage construction in \(\mathrm{thm{:}sharp\mbox{-}interval\mbox{-}price}\) strengthens (1): when \(k^*\geq3\),
\[
\frac{I^*}{k^*}\leq\frac{L+\lceil L/2\rceil-1}{3}<\frac L2. \tag{7}
\]
For \(k^*=1\), the ratio is \(1<L/2\).  Hence \(I^*/k^*=L/2\) can occur only for \(k^*=2\); in that case (1) shows that equality occurs exactly when \(I^*=L\).  Conversely, \(k^*=2\) and \(I^*=L\) plainly imply the ratio equality.

The arbitrary-set frontier gives
\[
k^*=2\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad R_1<\tau\leq R_2. \tag{8}
\]
Conditional on \(k^*=2\), the consecutive-hull argument behind (1) gives \(I^*\leq L\).  The interval frontier then gives
\[
I^*=L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad B_{L-1}<\tau, \tag{9}
\]
because the displayed strict inequality excludes every valid interval with at most \(L-1\) elements, while \(I^*\leq L\) supplies one with at most \(L\) elements.  Equations (8)--(9) prove the three-way low-coverage equivalence.  The quantities involved are finite maxima by the definition of the frontier profiles, so the characterization is computable and remains valid with zero cells and equality at the threshold.

We finally prove the existence claim for nonsymmetric high-coverage equality.  Necessity follows from (6): \(I^*=2L-1\) implies that all four endpoint masses exceed \(\alpha\).  In either arm, the two endpoint masses sum to at most one; hence \(2\alpha<1\).  This proves that such equality is impossible unless \(0<\alpha<1/2\), even without positivity or symmetry assumptions.

Conversely, fix \(0<\alpha<1/2\), choose
\[
0<\varepsilon<\min\{\alpha/4,(1-2\alpha)/4\},
\qquad M=\frac{1-\varepsilon}{2},
\qquad 0<\delta<M-\alpha,
\]
and define \(q=\mu_0\) and \(p=\mu_1\) by
\[
q_0=q_{L-1}=M,
\qquad p_0=M+\delta,
\qquad p_{L-1}=M-\delta,
\]
and
\[
p_i=q_i=\frac{\varepsilon}{L-2},
\qquad 1\leq i\leq L-2.
\]
Both vectors are normalized and strictly positive, and \(p\neq q\).  Also every endpoint mass exceeds \(\alpha\), so (6) gives \(B_{2L-2}<\tau\).  With \(A=B=\{0,L-1\}\),
\[
p(A)+q(B)=2(1-\varepsilon)>2-\alpha=\tau,
\]
and \(|A-B|=3\), whence \(R_3\geq\tau\).

To bound \(R_2\), inequality \(|A-B|\geq|A|+|B|-1\), proved in \(\mathrm{thm{:}sharp\mbox{-}interval\mbox{-}price}\), shows that \(|A-B|\leq2\) implies \(|A|+|B|\leq3\).  The two largest atoms of each marginal are its endpoints, because
\[
M-\delta>\alpha>\frac{\varepsilon}{L-2}.
\]
Therefore every rectangle entering \(R_2\) has mass sum at most
\[
(M+\delta)+(1-\varepsilon)
< (2M-\alpha)+(1-\varepsilon)
=2-2\varepsilon-\alpha
<2-\alpha=\tau.
\]
Thus \(R_2<\tau\).  The high-coverage equivalences already proved give \(k^*=3\) and \(I^*=2L-1\), establishing strictly positive nonsymmetric solutions for every and only \(0<\alpha<1/2\).  The elbow and lower-coverage examples asserted in the final sentence are exactly the normalized constructions verified in \(\mathrm{thm{:}sharp\mbox{-}interval\mbox{-}price}\), so their stated attainment properties follow.

theorem.statement:
Fix \(L\geq3\), \((\mu_0,\mu_1)\in\Delta_L^2\), and \(0<\alpha<1\).  Then
\[
\left\{\frac{I^*}{k^*}=\frac{2L-1}{3}\ \text{or}\ I^*-k^*=2L-4\right\}
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\left\{0<\alpha<\frac12,\ R_2<\tau\leq R_3,\ B_{2L-2}<\tau\right\}.
\]
On the right-hand side both equalities hold simultaneously, and
\[
B_{2L-2}<\tau
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\min\{\mu_{1,0},\mu_{1,L-1},\mu_{0,0},\mu_{0,L-1}\}>\alpha.
\]
Consequently, with every marginal cell positive, nonsymmetric simultaneous-equality solutions exist if and only if \(0<\alpha<1/2\); all of them are exactly the positive nonsymmetric pairs satisfying the displayed finite-profile inequalities.  One explicit family is obtained by choosing
\[
0<\varepsilon<\min\{\alpha/4,(1-2\alpha)/4\},
\quad M=(1-\varepsilon)/2,
\quad 0<\delta<M-\alpha,
\]
setting \(\mu_{0,0}=\mu_{0,L-1}=M\), \(\mu_{1,0}=M+\delta\), \(\mu_{1,L-1}=M-\delta\), and setting every interior cell in both arms equal to \(\varepsilon/(L-2)\).
theorem.proof_tex:
For \(0<\alpha<1/2\), \(\mathrm{thm{:}equality\mbox{-}regimes\mbox{-}characterized}\) proves that each of the two equalities on the left is equivalent to \(k^*=3\) and \(I^*=2L-1\), and that this pair of integer equalities is equivalent to
\[
R_2<\tau\leq R_3,
\qquad B_{2L-2}<\tau.
\]
It also computes
\[
B_{2L-2}=2-\min\{\mu_{1,0},\mu_{1,L-1},\mu_{0,0},\mu_{0,L-1}\},
\]
which, because \(\tau=2-\alpha\), proves the endpoint-mass equivalence in the statement.

It remains only to exclude the two high-coverage equalities when \(1/2\leq\alpha<1\).  The low-coverage part of \(\mathrm{thm{:}sharp\mbox{-}interval\mbox{-}price}\) gives
\[
\frac{I^*}{k^*}\leq\frac L2<\frac{2L-1}{3},
\]
where strictness uses \(L\geq3\).  Thus the ratio equality is impossible.  For the additive equality, if \(k^*=1\) then \(I^*-k^*=0\); if \(k^*=2\), then \(I^*\leq L\) and
\[
I^*-k^*\leq L-2<2L-4.
\]
If \(k^*\geq3\), the same theorem constructs an interval satisfying \(I^*\leq L+\lceil L/2\rceil-1\), so
\[
I^*-k^*\leq L+\lceil L/2\rceil-4<2L-4,
\]
because \(\lceil L/2\rceil<L\) for \(L\geq3\).  Hence the additive equality is also impossible in this regime.

Finally, the necessity argument in \(\mathrm{thm{:}equality\mbox{-}regimes\mbox{-}characterized}\) shows that simultaneous equality forces every endpoint mass to exceed \(\alpha\), and hence forces \(2\alpha<1\).  Its displayed \((\varepsilon,\delta)\) construction is normalized, strictly positive, and nonsymmetric and satisfies \(R_2<\tau\leq R_3\) and \(B_{2L-2}<\tau\) whenever \(0<\alpha<1/2\).  This proves both directions of the existence assertion and completes the inverse equality characterization.
